deck.title: Introductory Organic Chemistry

front_blocks.md: What is a **hazard** in a chemistry context?

back_blocks.md: A **hazard** is an inherent property of a chemical substance that has the potential to cause harm.

cards.front_md: What is a **hazard** in a chemistry context?
cards.back_md: A **hazard** is an inherent property of a chemical substance that has the potential to cause harm.

front_blocks.md: What is a **risk** in a chemistry context?

back_blocks.md: A **risk** is the chance that a hazard will actually cause harm, depending on how the substance is used.

cards.front_md: What is a **risk** in a chemistry context?
cards.back_md: A **risk** is the chance that a hazard will actually cause harm, depending on how the substance is used.

front_blocks.md: How does wearing eye protection affect the hazard and risk of using hydrochloric acid?

back_blocks.md: Wearing eye protection does not change the **hazard** of hydrochloric acid. It reduces the **risk** of the acid causing harm to your eyes.

cards.front_md: How does wearing eye protection affect the hazard and risk of using hydrochloric acid?

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The hazard of a substance changes depending on how you use it.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
The **hazard** relates to the inherent properties of the substance and does not change with use. It is the **risk** that changes depending on how the substance is used.

front_blocks.md: What does the **corrosive** hazard symbol warn about?

back_blocks.md: The **corrosive** symbol warns that the substance can cause skin burns and permanent eye damage.

cards.front_md: What does the **corrosive** hazard symbol warn about?

front_blocks.md: A substance labelled as having **acute toxicity** can cause **..........**  effects, even in small quantities.

back_blocks.md: A substance labelled as having **acute toxicity** can cause **life-threatening** effects, even in small quantities.

front_blocks.md: What is the purpose of a **risk assessment** in a laboratory?

back_blocks.md: A **risk assessment** identifies the hazards of substances being used, evaluates the risks associated with how they will be used, and sets out control measures to reduce those risks.

cards.front_md: What is the purpose of a **risk assessment** in a laboratory?
cards.back_md: A **risk assessment** identifies the hazards of substances being used, evaluates the risks associated with how they will be used, and sets out control measures to reduce those risks.

front_blocks.md: Give two factors a risk assessment might consider when deciding on control measures for a practical.

back_blocks.md: A risk assessment might consider:

1. Whether the substance will be **heated**
2. Whether **ventilation** or a **fume cupboard** is needed

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In an exam question about precautions, stating 'wear a lab coat and goggles' is always a sufficient answer.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

Wearing a lab coat and goggles is standard practice in any laboratory. A valid precaution must refer to the specific procedure, for example stating that a step producing HCl gas must be carried out in a **fume cupboard**.

front_blocks.md: Define **homologous series**

back_blocks.md: A **homologous series** is a group of organic compounds that share the same functional group, where each successive member differs by CH<sub>2</sub>.

cards.front_md: Define **homologous series**
cards.back_md: A **homologous series** is a group of organic compounds that share the same functional group, where each successive member differs by CH<sub>2</sub>.

front_blocks.md: Define **functional group**

back_blocks.md: A **functional group** is an atom or group of atoms within a molecule that determines the chemical and physical properties of that compound.

cards.front_md: Define **functional group**
cards.back_md: A **functional group** is an atom or group of atoms within a molecule that determines the chemical and physical properties of that compound.

front_blocks.md: What four features do all members of a homologous series share?

back_blocks.md: All members of a **homologous series**:

1. Have the same functional group
2. Have the same general formula
3. Have similar chemical properties
4. Differ by CH<sub>2</sub> between successive members

cards.front_md: What four features do all members of a homologous series share?
cards.back_md:

1. Have the same functional group
2. Have the same general formula
3. Have similar chemical properties
4. Differ by CH<sub>2</sub> between successive members

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Members of a homologous series have identical physical properties.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Members of a **homologous series** have gradually changing physical properties, such as boiling point, melting point and density, as the size of the molecule increases up the series.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

Members of a homologous series have identical physical properties.
cards.back_md:
**False.**

Members of a **homologous series** have gradually changing physical properties, such as boiling point, melting point and density, as the size of the molecule increases up the series.

front_blocks.md: Ethanol and propanol belong to the same **..........**  because they share the same functional group and differ by one CH<sub>2</sub> unit.

back_blocks.md: Ethanol and propanol belong to the same **homologous series** because they share the same functional group and differ by one CH<sub>2</sub> unit.

cards.front_md: Ethanol and propanol belong to the same **..........**  because they share the same functional group and differ by one CH<sub>2</sub> unit.
cards.back_md: Ethanol and propanol belong to the same **homologous series** because they share the same functional group and differ by one CH<sub>2</sub> unit.

front_blocks.md: Why do members higher in a homologous series tend to have higher boiling points?

back_blocks.md: As molecules increase in size up the series, there are more electrons and greater **London dispersion forces** between molecules. More energy is required to overcome these forces, so the boiling point increases.

cards.front_md: Why do members higher in a homologous series tend to have higher boiling points?
cards.back_md: As molecules increase in size up the series, there are more electrons and greater **London dispersion forces** between molecules. More energy is required to overcome these forces, so the boiling point increases.

front_blocks.md: What does the symbol R represent in the structural formula of a functional group?

back_blocks.md: **R** represents any other atom or group of atoms attached to the functional group, except for hydrogen.

cards.front_md: What does the symbol R represent in the structural formula of a functional group?
cards.back_md: **R** represents any other atom or group of atoms attached to the functional group, except for hydrogen.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
All members of a homologous series have similar chemical properties.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Because all members share the same **functional group**, they undergo similar chemical reactions and therefore have similar chemical properties.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

front_blocks.md: What does the stem 'but-' indicate in an organic compound name?

back_blocks.md: The stem **but-** indicates that the longest carbon chain in the molecule contains **4 carbon atoms**.

cards.front_md: What does the stem 'but-' indicate in an organic compound name?
cards.back_md: The stem **but-** indicates that the longest carbon chain in the molecule contains **4 carbon atoms**.

front_blocks.md: What is an **alkyl group**?

back_blocks.md: An **alkyl group** is a hydrocarbon side-chain derived from an alkane, formed by removing one hydrogen atom and named by adding '-yl' to the alkane stem (e.g. methyl, ethyl).

cards.front_md: What is an **alkyl group**?
cards.back_md: An **alkyl group** is a hydrocarbon side-chain derived from an alkane, formed by removing one hydrogen atom and named by adding '-yl' to the alkane stem (e.g. methyl, ethyl).

front_blocks.md: When numbering carbon atoms in a chain to name a compound, always start from the end that gives the **..........**  numbers in the name.

back_blocks.md: When numbering carbon atoms in a chain to name a compound, always start from the end that gives the **lowest possible** numbers in the name.

cards.front_md: When numbering carbon atoms in a chain to name a compound, always start from the end that gives the **..........**  numbers in the name.
cards.back_md: When numbering carbon atoms in a chain to name a compound, always start from the end that gives the **lowest possible** numbers in the name.

front_blocks.md: How is the prefix 'di-' used in IUPAC nomenclature?

back_blocks.md: The prefix **di-** is added in front of a substituent name to indicate that two identical alkyl groups or functional groups are present. Numbers indicating their positions are separated by a comma.

cards.front_md: How is the prefix 'di-' used in IUPAC nomenclature?
cards.back_md: The prefix **di-** is added in front of a substituent name to indicate that two identical alkyl groups or functional groups are present. Numbers indicating their positions are separated by a comma.

front_blocks.md: Define **addition reaction**

back_blocks.md: An **addition reaction** is an organic reaction in which two or more molecules combine to give a single product with no other products formed.

cards.front_md: Define **addition reaction**
cards.back_md: An **addition reaction** is an organic reaction in which two or more molecules combine to give a single product with no other products formed.

front_blocks.md: Define **elimination reaction**

back_blocks.md: An **elimination reaction** is a reaction in which a small molecule (such as H<sub>2</sub>O or HCl) is removed from an organic molecule.

cards.front_md: Define **elimination reaction**
cards.back_md: An **elimination reaction** is a reaction in which a small molecule (such as H<sub>2</sub>O or HCl) is removed from an organic molecule.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In a condensation reaction, two organic molecules join together with no other products formed.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
In a **condensation reaction**, two organic molecules join together but a small molecule such as H<sub>2</sub>O or HCl is also eliminated as a product.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

In a condensation reaction, two organic molecules join together with no other products formed.
cards.back_md:
**False.**

In a **condensation reaction**, two organic molecules join together but a small molecule such as H<sub>2</sub>O or HCl is also eliminated as a product.

front_blocks.md: In organic chemistry, what does the symbol [O] represent in a redox equation?

back_blocks.md: The symbol **[O]** represents one atom of oxygen from an **oxidising agent**. It is used to simplify equations for organic oxidation reactions without writing out the full oxidising agent.

cards.front_md: In organic chemistry, what does the symbol [O] represent in a redox equation?
cards.back_md: The symbol **[O]** represents one atom of oxygen from an **oxidising agent**. It is used to simplify equations for organic oxidation reactions without writing out the full oxidising agent.

front_blocks.md: What structural requirement must a monomer have to undergo addition polymerisation?

back_blocks.md: A monomer must contain at least one **C=C double bond** to undergo addition polymerisation. The double bond opens to allow monomers to link into a long-chain polymer.

cards.front_md: What structural requirement must a monomer have to undergo addition polymerisation?
cards.back_md: A monomer must contain at least one **C=C double bond** to undergo addition polymerisation. The double bond opens to allow monomers to link into a long-chain polymer.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
If an alkyl side-chain appears twice in a molecule, it is listed twice in alphabetical order.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
When the same alkyl group appears more than once, a multiplying prefix (**di-, tri-, tetra-**) is placed before its name. The group is only listed once in the name.

front_blocks.md: Define **structural isomers**

back_blocks.md: **Structural isomers** are compounds that have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae.

cards.front_md: Define **structural isomers**
cards.back_md: **Structural isomers** are compounds that have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae.

front_blocks.md: What is **chain isomerism**?

back_blocks.md: **Chain isomerism** is a type of structural isomerism where compounds have the same molecular formula but different lengths of longest carbon chain, caused by branching.

cards.front_md: What is **chain isomerism**?
cards.back_md: **Chain isomerism** is a type of structural isomerism where compounds have the same molecular formula but different lengths of longest carbon chain, caused by branching.

front_blocks.md: What is **positional isomerism**?

back_blocks.md: **Positional isomerism** is a type of structural isomerism where compounds have the same molecular formula and functional group, but the functional group is located on different carbon atoms.

cards.front_md: What is **positional isomerism**?
cards.back_md: **Positional isomerism** is a type of structural isomerism where compounds have the same molecular formula and functional group, but the functional group is located on different carbon atoms.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Propene and cyclopropane are structural isomers.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Both **propene** and **cyclopropane** have the molecular formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> but differ in their structural formulae, making them structural isomers.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

Propene and cyclopropane are structural isomers.
cards.back_md:
**True.**

Both **propene** and **cyclopropane** have the molecular formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> but differ in their structural formulae, making them structural isomers.

front_blocks.md: Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane are examples of **..........**  isomers because they have the same molecular formula but different lengths of longest carbon chain.

back_blocks.md: Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane are examples of **chain** isomers because they have the same molecular formula but different lengths of longest carbon chain.

cards.front_md: Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane are examples of **..........**  isomers because they have the same molecular formula but different lengths of longest carbon chain.
cards.back_md: Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane are examples of **chain** isomers because they have the same molecular formula but different lengths of longest carbon chain.

front_blocks.md: What is the difference between butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol, and what type of isomerism does this represent?

back_blocks.md: Both **butan-1-ol** and **butan-2-ol** have the molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O. They differ in the position of the hydroxyl group: it is on the first carbon in butan-1-ol and on the second carbon in butan-2-ol. This is **positional isomerism**.

cards.front_md: What is the difference between butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol, and what type of isomerism does this represent?
cards.back_md: Both **butan-1-ol** and **butan-2-ol** have the molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O. They differ in the position of the hydroxyl group: it is on the first carbon in butan-1-ol and on the second carbon in butan-2-ol. This is **positional isomerism**.

front_blocks.md: How does chain isomerism arise in organic molecules?

back_blocks.md: **Chain isomerism** arises through **branching** in the carbon skeleton. The same atoms are present but arranged so that the longest continuous carbon chain differs between isomers.

cards.front_md: How does chain isomerism arise in organic molecules?
cards.back_md: **Chain isomerism** arises through **branching** in the carbon skeleton. The same atoms are present but arranged so that the longest continuous carbon chain differs between isomers.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Structural isomers always have different molecular formulae.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
**Structural isomers** have the **same** molecular formula but different structural formulae. It is the arrangement of atoms that differs, not the overall composition.
